analogy.p: Think of each coulomb of charge as a delivery van and the potential difference as the amount of energy loaded into each van at the battery depot (joules per van). The charge flow Q is the number of vans that make the trip, so the total energy delivered is the number of vans times the energy per van: E = QV. The power is the energy delivered per second, so E = Pt is the total energy delivered if deliveries continue for time t. The analogy breaks down because charge carriers are not used up and do not carry the energy 'in a box' but transfer it through the electric field as they move.
analogy.t: Delivery vans carrying parcels of energy

bullets: Appliances transfer energy from the electrical supply to other energy stores; energy is conserved, never created or destroyed.
Useful energy transfer, for example thermal energy in a kettle; wasted energy transfer is dissipated to the surroundings (for example heating the cable and the air).
Energy transferred depends on power and time, so a small-power appliance left on for a long time can transfer more energy than a high-power appliance used briefly.
The unit of energy is the **joule (J)**; the energy transferred by a 1 W device in 1 s is 1 J.
The energy supplied by a circuit is transferred by moving charge through a potential difference, which is what E = QV describes.
Link to Energy topic: energy transferred = work done, so E = Pt is the same as W = Pt.
Link to Power note: P = VI and P = I²R give the power that goes into E = Pt.
core.p: Everyday electrical appliances are designed to bring about **energy transfers**. A kettle transfers electrical energy to the thermal energy store of the water, a motor transfers electrical energy to kinetic energy, a loudspeaker transfers electrical energy to sound, and a lamp transfers electrical energy to light (and wasted heat). The amount of energy an appliance transfers depends on how quickly it transfers energy (its power) and for how long it is switched on (its time). The specification asks you to calculate this energy with two equations, E = Pt and E = QV.

bullets: E = P t, with E in joules (J), P in watts (W), t in seconds (s).
Rearrangements: P = E / t and t = E / P.
Time must be in seconds when P is in watts: 2 minutes = 120 s; 1 hour = 3600 s.
Power must be in watts: 2.2 kW = 2200 W.
Worked idea: a 60 W lamp on for 10 s transfers 60 x 10 = 600 J.
A 1 kW heater running for 1 hour transfers 1000 x 3600 = 3 600 000 J = 3.6 MJ.
If power is constant, a graph of E against t is a straight line through the origin and its gradient is the power.
core.p: **Energy transferred (J) = power (W) x time (s)**. This is just the definition of power, P = E / t, rearranged. If you know the rate of energy transfer and how long it continues, multiply them to get the total energy transferred. The equation applies to any device, not just electrical ones, as long as the power is constant. For a changing power you would need to use the area under a power-time graph.

bullets: E = Q V, with E in joules, Q in coulombs (C) and V in volts (V).
Rearrangements: Q = E / V and V = E / Q.
1 volt means 1 joule of energy is transferred for every 1 coulomb of charge.
Example: a 12 V car battery moving 500 C transfers 500 x 12 = 6000 J.
Example: 3 C of charge passing through a component with a 9 V potential difference transfers 27 J.
The charge Q is found from Q = I t (charge flow = current x time).
A larger potential difference means more energy is transferred to the components per coulomb, for example a 230 V mains appliance compared with a 1.5 V cell.
core.p: **Energy transferred (J) = charge flow (C) x potential difference (V)**. Potential difference is defined as the energy transferred per unit charge, V = E / Q, so rearranging gives E = QV. When charge flows through a component, work is done on or by the charge: the charge gains energy from a cell or battery, and transfers that energy to the component. The more charge that flows, or the greater the potential difference, the more energy is transferred.

bullets: Q = I t, so I = Q / t and t = Q / I.
Time in seconds: a current of 2.0 A for 5 minutes gives Q = 2.0 x 300 = 600 C.
Current in amperes: 250 mA = 0.25 A.
In a series circuit, the same current flows at every point, so the same charge passes through each component in a given time.
The energy transferred by each component differs because the potential difference across each is different (E = QV).
Charge is conserved: it is not used up in the lamp; the energy it carries is transferred.
The coulomb is the unit of charge; one coulomb is the charge that passes a point in 1 s when the current is 1 A.
core.h: Charge, current and time: Q = It
core.p: To use E = QV you often need the charge, and the charge usually has to be calculated from the current and time. **Charge flow (C) = current (A) x time (s)**. A current of 1 ampere means 1 coulomb of charge passes a point every second. Remember that current is the rate of flow of charge, so the amount of charge that flows depends on how long the current flows for.

bullets: E = P t and P = V I give E = V I t.
Q = I t, so E = V x (I t) = V Q = Q V.
So the same energy can be found from E = Pt (with power and time) or E = QV (with charge and potential difference).
Example: a 6.0 V lamp with 2.0 A for 10 s: P = 12 W, so E = Pt = 120 J; Q = 20 C, so E = QV = 120 J. They match.
If you have V, I and t, you can use E = V I t directly.
Be careful to use the correct quantity for each: Q is charge in coulombs, not 'charge flow per second'.
This chain is a useful way to check the units: C x V = C x J/C = J.
core.h: Linking E = Pt and E = QV
core.p: The two energy equations give the same answer because they are connected by P = VI and Q = It. If you substitute P = VI into E = Pt you get E = VIt, and since It is the charge Q, E = VQ. This is a powerful check on a calculation and a good 'show that' route. It also demonstrates that power and potential difference are closely linked: power is the energy transferred per second, and potential difference is the energy transferred per coulomb.

bullets: 1 minute = 60 s; 1 hour = 3600 s; 1 day = 86 400 s.
Example: 3.0 kW for 2.0 minutes: E = 3000 x 120 = 360 000 J = 360 kJ.
Example check: 2 kJ in 4 s is a power of 2000 / 4 = 500 W.
Write standard form when numbers are large: 3.6 MJ = 3.6 x 10^6 J.
core.p: Energy is measured in **joules**, but the quantities in appliance questions are often given in kJ, kW or minutes, so unit conversions are a major source of lost marks. Always convert to base units (J, W, s, C, A, V) before substituting, and convert back at the end if the question asks for kJ or MJ.

bullets: Energy (kWh) = power (kW) x time (h).
Cost = energy in kWh x price per kWh (the price is given in the question, for example 28 p).
Do not mix: either use kW with hours (answer in kWh) or W with seconds (answer in J).
Example: 2.2 kW for 3 minutes = 0.05 h; E = 2.2 x 0.05 = 0.11 kWh; cost at 28 p/kWh is about 3.1 p.
Electricity meters in homes record the number of kWh used.
A heater that is 3 kW on for 2 h uses 6 kWh, which is much more than a 10 W lamp on for 2 h (0.02 kWh).
core.h: The kilowatt-hour and the cost of electricity
core.p: The joule is a very small unit, so domestic electricity is charged in **kilowatt-hours (kWh)**. A kilowatt-hour is the energy transferred by a 1 kW device operating for 1 hour. It is a unit of energy, not power. When power is in kilowatts and time in hours, energy in kWh is found by multiplying them: **energy (kWh) = power (kW) x time (h)**. The cost is the number of kWh multiplied by the price per kWh.

bullets: Higher power does not mean more energy: energy = power x time.
To compare energy costs, convert everything to kWh and multiply by the price.
Appliances with heating elements (kettle, toaster) have high power but are used for short times.
Appliances left on standby use a small power but a long time.
Reducing the time an appliance is on reduces the energy it transfers.
Reducing the power rating (for example an LED lamp rather than a filament lamp for the same light) reduces the energy transferred.
Use ratio reasoning: if power doubles and time halves, the energy is unchanged.
core.h: Comparing appliances: power, time and energy
core.p: A common exam idea is to compare two appliances. Power tells you how quickly each transfers energy, but the total energy depends on the time too. A 3 kW kettle running for 3 minutes transfers 0.15 kWh. A 100 W TV on for 3 hours transfers 0.30 kWh, so the TV transfers more energy even though its power is much lower. Always calculate the energy for each rather than comparing powers alone.

bullets: Efficiency = useful energy out / total energy in (= useful power out / total power in).
Efficiency is always less than 1 (or 100 per cent) for a real device.
A kettle is nearly 100 per cent efficient at heating water but wastes a little thermal energy to the surroundings.
A filament lamp is inefficient because most of the energy is transferred as thermal energy.
Wasted energy ends up in the thermal energy store of the surroundings, which is difficult to use again.
Insulation, lubrication and reducing air resistance reduce wasted energy.
Total energy supplied can be found from E = Pt (or E = QV), so efficiency calculations often start with this equation.
core.h: Efficiency of energy transfers in appliances
core.p: Not all of the energy supplied to an appliance is usefully transferred. Energy is conserved, so the total energy supplied equals the useful energy transferred plus the wasted energy (dissipated to the surroundings). Efficiency = useful energy transferred by the device / total energy supplied to the device, or the same ratio with powers. It is a ratio, so it has no unit, and is often expressed as a percentage.

bullets: Energy supplied electrically: E = V I t.
Energy stored thermally: change in thermal energy = mass x specific heat capacity x temperature change (E = m c delta-theta).
Ideal case: V I t = m c delta-theta, so c = V I t / (m delta-theta).
Measure V with a voltmeter in parallel and I with an ammeter in series.
Insulate the block or container to reduce energy dissipated to the surroundings.
Use a lid and stir water so the temperature is uniform.
Plot temperature against time; the gradient gives the rate of temperature rise.
Sources of error: heat loss, thermometer delay, power not constant, time reading errors.
core.h: Linking to the specific heat capacity practical
core.p: In the required practical on specific heat capacity, an electric heater supplies energy to a block or to water. The energy supplied is calculated from E = Pt, using P = VI from a voltmeter and ammeter reading and the time from a stopwatch. This is then compared with the energy needed to raise the temperature, E = m c delta-theta. If no energy were lost, the two would be equal; in practice some energy is dissipated to the surroundings, so the measured temperature rise is smaller than predicted.

bullets: E against t (constant P): straight line through the origin; gradient = P.
E against Q (constant V): straight line through the origin; gradient = V.
P against t: the area under the graph = energy transferred (E = Pt for a rectangle).
Use large triangles when calculating gradients and show the triangle on the graph.
State units for the gradient: kJ / s = kW; J / C = V.
If the line is curved, the power or potential difference is not constant.
Always read scales carefully (for example the axis may be in kJ or minutes).
Check the answer is sensible: a kettle energy for a few minutes is hundreds of kJ.
core.h: Graphs and data skills for energy transfer
core.p: Questions often present data or graphs involving energy, power, charge or time. For constant power the graph of energy against time is a straight line through the origin, and the gradient is the power. If the power changes, the energy transferred is the area under a power-time graph. Similarly the graph of energy against charge is a straight line and the gradient is the potential difference. Reading and interpreting these relationships correctly is a typical 3 or 4 mark skill.

bullets: A 1.5 V cell gives 1.5 J to each coulomb of charge.
Battery packs in series add their potential differences, so the energy per coulomb increases.
The energy transferred from a cell in time t is E = V I t.
The larger the current drawn, the faster the cell runs down.
Recharging a rechargeable cell reverses the energy transfer, with some wasted as thermal energy.
Energy transferred to the external circuit is shared in the ratio of the component resistances in a series circuit.
In a parallel circuit, the charge from the cell splits, but each coulomb still gains energy equal to the cell's potential difference.
core.p: A cell or battery transfers chemical energy to the charge carriers. The potential difference of the cell tells you the energy given to each coulomb. If a charge Q passes through a cell of potential difference V, the energy given to the charge is E = QV. This energy is then transferred to the components in the external circuit (for example as thermal energy in a resistor or light and heat in a lamp). The chemical store of the cell decreases accordingly.

bullets: Ammeter in **series** (it has a very small resistance, so it does not change the current).
Voltmeter in **parallel** across the component (it has a very large resistance, so it takes almost no current).
Time must be in **seconds** before using E = P t or Q = I t.
Current and p.d. must be steady during the measurement; if they change, use average values or split the time into intervals.
A graph of E against t for a constant power is a straight line through the origin; the gradient is the power.
A graph of E against Q for a constant p.d. is a straight line through the origin; the gradient is the p.d.
In circuit diagrams the cell or battery symbol uses a **long line for the positive terminal** and a short line for the negative.
Conventional current flows from the positive terminal round the circuit to the negative terminal.
core.h: Measuring the quantities: ammeter, voltmeter and stopwatch
core.p: To find the energy transferred by a component you measure the three quantities in E = V I t. The **ammeter** is connected **in series** so that the same current flows through it as through the component, and the **voltmeter** is connected **in parallel** across the component so that it measures the potential difference between its ends. A stopwatch measures the time. The charge flow is then found from Q = I t and the energy from E = Q V. Choosing the right meter position matters in the exam: a voltmeter in series would almost stop the current because its resistance is very large, and an ammeter in parallel would act almost like a short circuit.

bullets: 1 volt = 1 joule per coulomb (1 V = 1 J/C).
For the same charge flow, doubling the p.d. doubles the energy transferred.
For the same p.d., doubling the charge flow doubles the energy transferred.
Charge flow Q = I t, so a larger current or a longer time means more charge passes and more energy is transferred.
Energy is transferred **from** the battery's chemical store **to** the components, then dissipated to the surroundings.
The same current flows at every point in a series circuit, but the p.d. is shared between the components.
Total energy transferred in the whole circuit equals the energy supplied by the battery (conservation of energy).
E = V I t is the combined form, and since P = V I it is the same as E = P t.
core.h: Why a higher potential difference transfers more energy
core.p: Potential difference is defined as the **energy transferred per unit charge**, V = E / Q, so a p.d. of 12 V means that each coulomb of charge transfers 12 joules of energy as it passes through the component. That is why the equation E = Q V is correct: if every coulomb transfers V joules, then Q coulombs transfer Q x V joules. At a battery the chemical store does work on the charge, giving each coulomb some energy; in a component such as a motor or lamp the charge gives that energy to other stores (kinetic, thermal, light). The charge itself is not used up, it continues round the circuit, and it is the energy that is moved between stores.

exam: Command words: 'Calculate' needs equation, substitution and unit; 'Show that' needs working that arrives at the given value to more significant figures than the answer; 'Explain' needs a reason.
2-mark calculation pattern: 1 mark for correct equation and substitution (E = 2200 x 180), 1 mark for the answer and unit (396 000 J).
Always check the units in the question: kW, minutes, mA and kJ must be converted unless you are working in kWh.
For cost questions (usually 3 marks) calculate kWh = kW x h, then multiply by the price per kWh, then give the unit (p or pounds).
E = QV questions often give a current and a time first: calculate Q = It, then E = QV.
Use the phrase 'energy is transferred' (never 'used up'), and 'dissipated to the surroundings' for waste.

'Explain why the temperature rise is lower than predicted' (2 marks): some energy is dissipated to the surroundings; so not all the electrical energy supplied is transferred to the thermal energy store of the water.
Graph questions: gradient of an energy-time graph = power; gradient of an energy-charge graph = potential difference. Draw a large triangle.
A 4 to 6 mark comparison question: calculate the energy for each appliance, compare numerically, and conclude using the numbers.
Check that the answer is reasonable: a kettle for a few minutes transfers hundreds of kJ, a mobile phone charge transfers a few tens of kJ.
Required skills: draw a circuit with correct symbols, put the ammeter in series and the voltmeter in parallel, then use E = V I t or E = Q V with Q = I t; state the unit at each step.

mistakes.r: Convert to W and s first (or use kW and h to get kWh).
mistakes.w: Leaving power in kW and time in minutes in E = Pt

mistakes.r: Energy is in joules (J); power is in watts (W); cost uses kWh.
mistakes.w: Using the wrong unit: giving energy in W or power in J

mistakes.r: A kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy: kW x h.
Compare the energy transferred, E = Pt, which also depends on the time.
Q is charge in coulombs; find it from Q = It first.
mistakes.w: Using E = QV with current instead of charge

mistakes.r: Energy is transferred to other stores and dissipated to the surroundings; the total is conserved.
mistakes.w: Saying energy is 'used up' by the appliance

mistakes.r: Cost = number of kWh x price per kWh, quoted with units (p or pounds).
mistakes.w: Forgetting to multiply by the price per kWh for the cost

mistakes.r: Write the equation, substitute with units, then give the final answer with unit to earn method marks.
mistakes.w: Not showing the equation and substitution
Using minutes in the formula without converting

mistakes.r: Ammeter in series with the component; voltmeter in parallel across it.
mistakes.w: Connecting the voltmeter in series (or the ammeter in parallel) in a circuit diagram

summary: The specification asks you to calculate the energy transferred by an appliance using E = Pt and by moving charge through a potential difference using E = QV (with Q = It), including units, kilowatt-hours and cost. It matters because energy-transfer and cost calculations appear regularly in Paper 1 and link to efficiency and the specific heat capacity practical.

terms.d: The amount of energy moved from one store to another or from one place to another, in joules.
The unit of energy; the energy transferred when a power of 1 watt operates for 1 second.
The rate at which energy is transferred or work is done; P = E / t.
A rate of energy transfer of one joule per second.
The energy transferred when a force moves an object or a charge flows through a potential difference.
The amount of electric charge passing a point, measured in coulombs; Q = It.
The unit of charge; the charge that passes when a current of 1 ampere flows for 1 second.
The energy transferred per unit charge, V = E / Q; measured in volts.
The unit of potential difference; one joule of energy transferred per coulomb of charge.
The rate of flow of electric charge; I = Q / t.
The energy transferred by a 1 kW appliance operating for 1 hour; equal to 3.6 million joules.
Useful energy (or power) output divided by total energy (or power) input.
Energy spread out to the surroundings, usually as thermal energy, so that it is wasted.
The energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 degree Celsius.
Energy can be transferred, stored or dissipated, but cannot be created or destroyed.
A unit of power equal to 1000 watts; used with hours to give kilowatt-hours.
A meter connected in series that measures the current in a circuit, in amperes.
A meter connected in parallel across a component that measures the potential difference, in volts.
The unit of current; a current of 1 A transfers a charge of 1 coulomb each second.

worked.ans: (a) 396 000 J (396 kJ); (b) 0.11 kWh costing about 3.1 p.
worked.q: A 2.2 kW kettle is switched on for 3.0 minutes. (a) Calculate the energy transferred in joules. (b) Calculate the energy in kWh and the cost if electricity costs 28 p per kWh. [5 marks]
steps: (a) P = 2.2 kW = 2200 W; t = 3.0 minutes = 180 s.
Cost = 0.11 x 28 = 3.08 p, which is about 3.1 p.
Check: 0.11 kWh x 3.6 MJ per kWh = 0.396 MJ = 396 000 J, matching part (a).

worked.q: A 12 V battery is connected to a motor. A current of 2.0 A flows for 4.0 minutes. Calculate (a) the charge that flows, (b) the energy transferred. [4 marks]
steps: Check using E = V I t = 12 x 2.0 x 240 = 5760 J, so the answers agree.
Power check: P = V I = 24 W; 24 x 240 = 5760 J.

worked.ans: Temperature rise = 75 degrees C (an ideal value; in practice it would be lower because some energy is dissipated to the surroundings).
worked.q: A 1.5 kW immersion heater is placed in 2.0 kg of water and switched on for 7.0 minutes. Assuming no energy is wasted, calculate the temperature rise of the water. (Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg/degree C.) [4 marks]
steps: E = m c delta-theta, so delta-theta = E / (m c) = 630 000 / (2.0 x 4200).
